patient.chief_complaint: Progressive confusion and memory difficulty with constipation and recent opioid use
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 64-year-old Asian man with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 22) awaiting DAA therapy who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion and memory difficulty over 72 hours. The wife reports he has been increasingly confused since three days ago. He has not had a bowel movement in 5 days and has been in abdominal pain from severe constipation. The wife reveals that she gave him extra codeine phosphate 30 mg doses — up to 4 doses per day over the past 3 days — for his abdominal pain from constipation. He is prescribed codeine PRN; the wife was not aware it could be harmful for him. The ammonia on admission is 164 µmol/L. EEG shows classic triphasic waves. There is no fever and the WBC is normal. The urine drug screen is positive for codeine/opiates.

output.query: Direct-acting antiviral therapy in hepatitis C cirrhosis — effect on hepatic encephalopathy

results.title: SVR with direct-acting antivirals in HCV cirrhosis reduces hepatic encephalopathy recurrence
results.finding: Achieving SVR12 with DAA therapy in compensated and decompensated HCV cirrhosis significantly reduces HE recurrence, improves MELD score (approximately 2-4 points reduction), and reduces liver-related mortality. AASLD/IDSA guidelines recommend DAA therapy in all patients with HCV cirrhosis regardless of decompensation status. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (8 weeks) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (12 weeks) are preferred pan-genotypic regimens for decompensated cirrhosis.
results.relevance: High — initiate DAA after HE stabilization (decompensated cirrhosis may have drug-related hepatotoxicity risk — use Child-Pugh-appropriate regimen; avoid ribavirin in Child-Pugh C)

output.summary: Sustained virological response with direct-acting antiviral therapy in HCV cirrhosis is associated with reduced HE recurrence, improved MELD score, and reduced liver-related mortality. Pangenotypic DAA regimens are preferred for decompensated cirrhosis per current AASLD/IDSA guidelines. Regimen selection should account for Child-Pugh class and genotype. Clinical correlation recommended.

MELD_Transplant.value: HCV genotype 1a — curable with DAA pre-transplant; post-transplant recurrence prevention with short-course DAA also possible

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 22) — precipitated by constipation and codeine accumulation (opioid in liver disease); ammonia 164.

differential.key_features: Tox screen positive for codeine/opiates; opioids both directly depress consciousness and precipitate HE through constipation and CNS depression.

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs: CMP including AST/ALT/bilirubin/INR/albumin, ammonia, CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), BUN/Cr, lactate, blood cultures and urine cultures; toxicology if substance use plausible. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 164; tox positive for codeine; cirrhosis features.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (AASLD/EASL HE; opioid use in cirrhosis; constipation as HE precipitant).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering codeine (DISCONTINUE), lactulose, rifaximin; substitute non-opioid analgesia (acetaminophen at hepatic-safe doses); flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — consider if no improvement with opioid hold and lactulose. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult hepatology and pain medicine for non-opioid alternatives; expedite DAA therapy — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Discontinue codeine; replace with acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing (max 2-3 g/day).
Lactulose to 2-4 stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BID.
Expedite DAA therapy planning once acute HE resolves.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not give NSAIDs in cirrhosis (renal failure risk).
Avoid all opioids unless absolutely necessary; if essential, use low-dose, short-acting and add aggressive lactulose.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Opioids precipitate HE via both direct CNS depression and constipation; codeine specifically has reduced clearance in cirrhosis and accumulates.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward HE: hepatitis C cirrhosis with constipation and codeine accumulation as dual precipitants; opioids contraindicated in cirrhosis; partial naloxone reversal distinguishes opioid vs ammonia contribution
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools; dual precipitants (constipation + codeine) but the trigger is unambiguous from medication history; minimal distractors.
